comments.rawMarkdown:
In my view, Tufa Labs and Yi-Chia Chen are unlikely to share their solutions right now, especially if claiming the prize would require them to disclose their training data, base model, or other core resources that they may have spent significantly more money and effort developing.

For the other teams, I suspect much of the progress is still centered around optimizing existing harnesses, prompting strategies, and agent frameworks, rather than relying on major breakthroughs. In that case, teams currently scoring around 10.x–20.x may have a strong incentive to open-source their code and claim the Milestone #2 prize.

I don’t think most agents in the 10.x–20.x range currently have a huge, hard-to-replicate technical advantage. Once Milestone #2 is over and more solutions become public, the gap could close very quickly, and many of these agents may be surpassed soon afterward.

comments.rawMarkdown:
Two things to bear in mind:
1. If both teams manage to remain at the top until the end of the competition, one team must take the second position and the prize money is $15k, which is less than the milestone 2 first place prize money ($25k). They will NOT both win $40k at the end, Unless they're not interested in the money.
2. A big AI company can release a very powerful open weight model that can fit into the RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell, and other teams will match or surpass their performance if their performance has no unique architectural design, but solely depends on model capabilities.

- What do you think will happen when teams with scores ranging from 21-27 share their full code now? Looking forward to your comments..
